1:
Why Benjamin is addressed rather than Judah is answered alike by four of them. Gill notes that the tribe stayed with Judah when the ten tribes revolted, that part of Jerusalem lay in its territory, and that the prophet was born within it. Ellicott says the city, though claimed for Judah, stood on the border of the two, the boundary running through the valley of Hinnom and the northern walls in Benjamin, so it was natural for a prophet of that village to speak of it as his own. Wesley gives the same reason, Calvin adding that the prophet addresses his kindred first.

The signals are located on the map by three of them. Ellicott reads the trumpet at Tekoa as the order for the fugitives to halt, but not till they reach the southernmost boundary of Judah, twelve miles south of the city. Wesley calls it one of the fenced cities built by an early king, glosses the sign as a fired beacon, and translates the second place-name as the house of the vineyard, a tower raised among the vines. Clarke sets the scene in the prophet's vision: seeing the invaders on the march, he bids his people set up the signals of distress. Henry stresses the contrast the alarm interrupts: the city and country were secure and saw no cloud gathering, everything safe and serene, when they were told of an invasion that would cause not consternation only but desolation.

Calvin explains the manner of the passage. Punishment is not merely announced as near but set before the eyes, because men are wholly thoughtless whenever God threatens and reproofs make no impression, so vivid descriptions are needed and the event must be represented as present. He accounts for the pastoral idiom biographically: the prophet's birthplace was pastoral and he kept the expressions of his upbringing, God not having divested his servants of natural endowment when he appointed them to teach.

The comparison of the daughter of Zion is the tile's one textual dispute. Gill takes it of a woman dwelling at home in ease and security, which describes the secure state of the people, and reports two Jewish commentators supplying woman as the English does; others supply land or pasture, making the nation the pastures that invite shepherds, and a third rendering turns the clause into an address, O beautiful and delicate one, I have destroyed the daughter of Zion. Ellicott presses the point harder. The word woman is not in the Hebrew, and the term rendered comely is elsewhere translated fold or habitation, so the passage should read that the daughter of Zion is likened to a fair pasturage, setting up the imagery of the next verse; he too records the vocative alternative. Calvin leaves it open, doubting whether the prophet compares her to a tender maid or means something else.

On the shepherds all are agreed and the gloss is uniform. Gill has kings and their armies, following the Targum, generals compared to shepherds and their forces to flocks. Clarke says the chiefs and their battalions, come to spoil the fertile fields. Wesley names the Chaldean princes coming into that pleasant land. Keil and Delitzsch make the figure stand for princes who with their peoples besiege and sack the city, rejecting one scholar's suggestion of a nomad swarm or a particular northern people. Ellicott corrects the pronoun to the pasture rather than to her, notes the following verbs stand in the past because the future is seen as realised, and reads the last clause as each letting his hand rove in plunder beside his tent, the imagery drawn from a nomadic tribe attacking a cultivated plain. Calvin draws the moral: there is no ground for the people to deceive themselves because God has spared them so far, since the city would now be so far in the enemy's power that each would choose his own portion.
4:
The summons to prepare war is a technical term and two of them say so. Ellicott corrects the rendering to sanctify, noting that the opening of a battle was accompanied by sacrifices, divinations and prayers, and points to the practice both of Israel and of the Chaldeans, the latter being present to the prophet's mind. Calvin says the same from the Hebrew idiom, that in every age wars were proclaimed by a solemn rite, a feeling God has implanted in all nations. He also marks the change of manner: the prophet leaves the similitude of shepherds and describes the enemies directly, and by a kind of personification introduces the Chaldeans encouraging one another to fight, having until now spoken as God's herald proclaiming war. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same transition, from figure to reality, with the enemies appearing as speakers who incite one another to storm the city, and explain the consecration as undertaken because the war was under commission from God.

Who speaks the words is left unsettled. Gill offers either the Lord calling the Chaldeans in his providence or the invaders stirring one another up, and prefers the second on the strength of what follows. Wesley takes them the other way, as God's own summons, and reads the eagerness as showing how ready they will be to obey the call. Clarke has them impatient lest any time be lost and the besieged gain leisure to strengthen themselves or get in supplies. Ellicott makes their haste vivid: so eager that instead of resting at noon for the midday meal they would press on to the assault.

The complaint about the failing day is turned into arithmetic by Calvin, who counts the hours. From midday to nightfall is six hours, the day being divided into twelve with the first beginning at sunrise; so the sense is that since the city cannot be taken in six hours they will attack by night. He calls the description graphic and says the enemies were urged on by the hidden power of God. Gill reads it the same way, that having failed by day they propose the night, losing no time but proceeding day and night until they accomplish their end. Clarke turns it into their own reasoning: having lost the day let them not lose the night, but take advantage of the darkness while the defenders are under the impression of terror. Wesley draws the same inference, that losing neither day nor night shows they were extraordinarily stirred up by God.
6:
The siege works are described from the monuments. Ellicott says the words graphically render the process of an Eastern siege as seen in the Assyrian reliefs: first the neighbouring country is cleared by cutting the trees, then a mound is raised, either by piling earth on the timber as a framework or with earth alone, until it reaches the level of the wall, and then the assault is made. Clarke gives the same two steps more briefly, timber for machines and a mound to overlook the city for the engines, and puts a sentence in the besiegers' mouths, that they are sure of success because God will deliver the city into their hands. Gill and Wesley both make the theological point the verse turns on: the whole affair was of the Lord, who brought the Chaldeans from their country and directed them, so that they were an army under his command and the Jews had more to fear from the Lord of armies than from the army itself. Calvin states the same purpose as one of two things needing to be done, the first being to expose the stupidity by which the people disregarded every threatening, and the second to make them know they had to do not with the Chaldeans but with God himself.

The fountain casting out its waters is glossed simply by three and made difficult by one. Gill has the wickedness poured out in great abundance and continually; Clarke says the inhabitants are incessant in their acts of iniquity and do nothing but sin; Calvin amplifies the earlier charge that the city was a den of thieves, and draws the distinction that many vices may break out of a place and repentance follow, but when men cease not and heap vices on vices it appears that they swell with wickedness. Ellicott finds two difficulties in the Hebrew, that the word rendered fountain is better a cistern and is not spelt with the usual vowels, and that the etymology of the verb is quite uncertain, so that it has been rendered as gathering, keeping in, keeping cool, or letting flow; he thinks the received version probably gives the general meaning, and corrects grief to sickness.

The appeal that follows is read by all as genuine and by two as affecting. Gill corrects instructed to corrected, and finds in it the divine affection notwithstanding their sins, that their amendment and not their destruction was pleasing, that the visitation was undertaken with reluctance, and that even now it was not too late. Clarke says plainly that there is still respite, and that a wholehearted return would arrest the advancing army on its march and turn it back. Ellicott corrects the same word to chastened and renders the next clause more strongly, that the divine soul may tear itself away. Wesley catches the same force, calling the word a most emphatic metaphor by which God expresses how great a grief it is to withdraw, like separating one limb from another. Calvin hears God stopping in mid-course of his wrath and asking what is to be done, whether he shall destroy the city he has chosen, and attributes to him a paternal feeling, unwilling to proceed to extreme rigour against his own people.
9:
The gleaning is understood by all as a figure of exhaustive plunder, and the details are supplied by different hands. Calvin insists on the exact sense of the verb, which means not to gather the vintage but to glean after it: as after harvest the poor pick up ears here and there until nothing remains in the field, so a gleaning of the vines leaves nothing. Wesley draws the consequence, that Judah shall be gleaned over and over until there is a full end, the enemy not content with one spoiling but returning a second and a third time to carry off persons and plunder. Clarke reads the command as addressed to the invaders, to turn back and glean the remnant left after the capture, since even that remnant did not profit by the judgments fallen on the rest. Henry describes the havoc the war makes, the enemy quartering so long among them and so insatiable in their thirst after blood and treasure that what escapes at one time falls into their hands at another. Gill notes where in the discourse it comes, when all the threatenings and admonitions had proved vain.

The clause about turning back the hand is where the readings differ most. Ellicott takes the grape-gatherer carrying his work to the last grape or tendril as a parable of unsparing desolation, and holds the command addressed to the minister of destruction, whether the Babylonian king or the angel of death; the noun rendered baskets occurs here only and probably means, like a kindred word in another prophet, the tendrils on which the gatherer's hand was to be turned. Keil and Delitzsch render it the same way, laying the hand again as a vine-dresser on the shoots, and state the ground of judgment: it falls unsparingly because the people listen to no warning but are confirmed in shameless courses by false prophets and wicked priests. Calvin makes the verse an answer to an objection: God dreaded a sight so mournful which the Jews disregarded, and his late exhortation to repent was not in vain, since he foresaw how dreadful their calamities would be.

The prophet's own question in the next verse is read as despair by some and as a formal difficulty by others. Gill takes it as despair of any success by his ministry, the people so universally depraved that none would hear, speaking being only beating the air and every warning signifying nothing. Calvin sets the question against what precedes and answers the apparent contradiction: he had just said God was still ready to be reconciled if they repented, and now says his words were wholly lost, asking as of something unexpected; there is nothing inconsistent, since he wished so far as he could to secure their safety. Keil and Delitzsch resolve it the same way and add the prophet's compulsion: he might warn the people once more to turn the judgment away, but they cannot and will not hear, being utterly hardened, and yet he cannot be silent, so filled with the fury of God that he must pour it forth.

The uncircumcised ear is glossed by three. Ellicott sets it beside the other members scripture calls uncircumcised, the lips and the heart, taking it to mean the ear had never been brought into covenant or consecrated; he identifies the speaker as the prophet in his own name, who has heard the message but asks who will listen. Wesley distinguishes the two figures, an uncircumcised ear signifying the rejecting of instruction and an uncircumcised heart an obstinate and rebellious will, and is careful about the incapacity: they had brought themselves under it by their own obstinacy and wilfulness. On the last clause Ellicott glosses the reproach as the object of their scorn, Clarke says it is an object of derision which they despise, and Wesley that they laugh at it.
11:
Whose fury the prophet is full of divides the tile at once. Gill offers either a zeal for the glory of God's name, or, following the Targum, the prophecy concerning the wrath to come for their sins. Calvin allows the same ambiguity in another form, that the phrase may be taken passively or actively: either the prophet was indignant with holy zeal because he had undertaken God's cause, or he dreaded the judgment the Jews took no notice of. He explains why the tone rises here: it was not enough to set the truth before refractory men, but necessary to stimulate them sharply and sometimes to wound them, nothing else being able to rouse so great a hardness. Clarke makes it the burden of the revelation, that God had given him a dreadful sight of the judgments intended and his soul was weighed down by the prophecy, which he had endeavoured to suppress. Wesley says he is filled with the fire of God's wrath, which he must discharge.

Ellicott alone corrects the mood of the next clause. The prophet feels himself filled, frail vessel as he is, with a wrath that will not be controlled; but the words that follow are better taken as a command from the mouth of God, pour it out. He reads the list as the stages of a man's life over which the torrent flows, the children abroad meaning those playing in the streets, the gathering of young men taken either of their mirth or of secret counsels. Wesley reads the same list plainly, noting that the streets are where children sport, that one sex as well as the other shall be a prey, and that those full of days were at the edge of the grave. Clarke gives the same catalogue and insists all must partake.

The transfer of houses and fields is treated as the result rather than a new charge. Keil and Delitzsch state it so: the verse gives the result of being taken, houses and fields and wives handed over to others. Gill says the same, transferred to strangers as their property. Calvin makes the loss of the land the point of the vengeance and explains why it strikes at their confidence. Because it had been said, this is my rest for ever, here will I dwell, they imagined they could not be driven out and thought their dwelling as certain as the sun and moon in the heavens; so the prophet says their houses would go to foreigners.

The universality of the corruption is where the tile does its plainest work. Gill takes from the least to the greatest not of age but of station, from the lowest class to those in the highest places of trust, so that since men of every station had sinned it was just that all should share the common calamity. Calvin reports the alternative that it might be understood of young and old, but prefers the first clause of the lower orders and the second of the higher ranks, the point being that contempt of God prevailed not in one part only but throughout. Ellicott presses the word rendered given to covetousness, literally gained gain, which does not necessarily involve dishonest gain though that is often implied; what is condemned is the universal desire of gain, sure to lead to its gratification by fair means or foul. He then makes the sharpest observation here: the two orders that ought to have checked the evil are singled out as foremost in promoting it. Wesley reads the same clause as doing falsehood, as if that were their whole work, the proper sin of priests and prophets being to deceive the people and flatter them with false visions. Keil and Delitzsch carry it forward to the healing of the hurt slightly, the crying of peace where there is none, and the shamelessness that could not blush.
14:
The slight healing is the governing figure, worked hardest by Gill. The false prophets and lying priests pretended to be physicians and to cure the distempered state of the people, and did so in their way but not thoroughly: they did not search the wound to the bottom but drew a skin over it and called that a cure. Ellicott renders the adverb literally, as a thing of nought, and makes the comparison exact: the false prophets were as physicians who told a man with a fatal disease he was in full health, peace being taken almost as health. He notes that the words of the daughter stand in italics because the marginal reading omits them. Clarke calls those words improperly added here, though found in some manuscripts; the cry itself promised prosperity when there was none and when God had determined there should be none. Wesley refers the charge peculiarly to the prophets, who daubed over the coming misery by persuading the people it would not come, or would be easily cured. Calvin restricts it to the prophets and priests too, adding that they not only corrupted the people by their example but shook off every fear of God and by their impostures took away all respect for true teaching; he reports how three ancient versions render the disputed phrase, as regarding it as nothing, with reproach, and with mockery.

The shamelessness that follows is read as a formal grammatical question by one and as a moral state by the rest. Ellicott is the most exact: the Hebrew gives an assertion, not a question, that they are brought to shame because they have committed abominations, and the following verb, in a different voice, adds that even so they were not ashamed. There was no inward shame even when they were covered with ignominy; they had lost the power to blush, then as always the most hopeless of states, and falling among those that fall was its sequel. Gill refers the charge first to the false prophets and priests, who when reproved for the idolatry into which they had led others were not ashamed, being given up to judicial hardness. Calvin observes that the address widens here from priests and prophets to the whole people, sufficiently proved guilty, their disgrace visible to heaven and earth, and yet so fronted that no sense of shame touches them, which means the wickedness was past remedy. Wesley notes only that they sinned by encouraging the people and joining them.

The standing in the ways is a parable everyone expands, and they differ in what the traveller does. Wesley has travellers in doubt of their road stand still and consider whether a false guide's direction is right. Gill takes it as a summons to judge for themselves rather than be blindly led: where two ways meet a man makes a short stop and looks to the way-post which points where each path leads, and in religion the scriptures are that way-mark. Clarke tells it as a narrative: the traveller comes where the road divides, stops short and cannot fix his choice until he meets another, inquires, gets directions, proceeds, arrives and reposes after his fatigue; he adds that an excellent sermon on the words stands among the tales of the first English poet. Ellicott reads the people as a traveller on a self-chosen path that leads to peril, and presses the phrase old paths, which he renders the eternal paths, going beyond the mere antiquity of the nation's life; of these they were to choose the one most distinctly the good way. Keil and Delitzsch state the doctrinal point: judgment cannot be turned aside by sacrifice without a change of heart. Calvin adds the use: the fault could not be extenuated as ignorance, since they had been warned more than enough and would not so much as open their eyes.
17:
The watchmen are identified with the prophets by everyone, and the identification is defended two ways. Gill reports two Jewish commentators glossing them as prophets, notes that the Targum interprets them teachers, and extends the office to the apostles and to all faithful preachers who watch for souls and warn of danger. Clarke says the same in eight words. Keil and Delitzsch ground it in usage, watchmen being those who stand on the watch-tower to keep a lookout and warn the people by proclaiming what they have seen in spirit; they add that the summons to hearken is not spoken by the watchmen themselves. Ellicott takes the figure from war: these are the sentinels of an army, giving the signal not for advance but for retreat, blowing the trumpet of alarm to proclaim the nearness of the invader and calling the people to flee. They call in vain.

Calvin explains why the trumpet aggravates the charge rather than merely repeating it. The people were not only deaf to admonitions but would not be roused by a trumpet or even attend to it; and the trumpet ought to have penetrated their minds more than anything for two reasons, being louder than any human voice, and not commonly heard except when war is at hand. Wesley reads the trumpet as the voice of the prophet, marking his loud crying on account of imminent danger.

The appeal to the nations is where the tile finds a genuine textual difficulty. Keil and Delitzsch say the sense of the clause addressed to the congregation is far from clear and has been very variously given; several scholars understand it of an assembly of foreign nations, but the word cannot bear that without some qualifier, and a second mention of the nations would be out of place. Ellicott sets out a threefold appeal, to the heathen nations, then to the congregation of Israel or possibly of mankind, and third to the earth as witness of the judgments; he corrects the last clause to what comes to pass for them, that is, for the sinful people. Gill reads the summons as itself a rebuke: since the Jews refused to hear, the Gentiles are called on, and it shames them that these would hear when they would not. Calvin makes the same point at length and calls the shame very great: the nations addressed had never heard anything of true religion, while the Jews had been taught by the law and the prophets and had the same things repeated morning and evening, so that more understanding was found among the heathen. Henry reads it as an appeal to the equity of the proceedings, addressed to the neighbours and to the whole world, particularly the great men who take cognizance of the affairs of states around them and wonder that such evil should fall on this people. Wesley says the nations are called as spectators of the severity, the greatness of the punishment answering the greatness of the sins.

The last appeal is to the earth, and the reason given is uniform. Gill has the earth and its inhabitants called to witness the righteousness of the procedure, the evil of punishment answering to the evil of sin. Calvin explains why the address turns outward: God would have spoken directly to the Jews had they ears, but their contempt had made them deaf, so it was necessary to address the earth; the testimony given is that he would not act cruelly, rewarding them only as they deserved, so that however grievous the punishment they could not complain. Keil and Delitzsch fix on the phrase that names the evil, fruit of their thoughts rather than of their deeds, and say the wording is chosen to mark the hostility of the evil heart toward God; they note too that the law is given prominence by the turn of the expression.
20:
The imported incense is located geographically and then dismissed theologically. Gill places the source in Persia or Arabia, whence the best incense was brought, and says the offering was of no esteem while the prophet's words were despised. Clarke fixes it toward the southern extremity of the Arabian peninsula, a far country in relation to Judea, famous for the best incense, and identifies the sweet cane as the aromatic calamus which yields a fine smell when dried and pulverised and was used in making the holy anointing oil. Ellicott adds the literary pedigree, that this land had a proverbial fame for gold and frankincense alike, and cites a Latin poet and a later English one for its odours, together with the queen who brought spices and gold; on the cane he prefers literally the good cane, one of the ingredients of the temple incense. Wesley locates it in the same region and puts the question bluntly: to what purpose is all this trouble and charge to fetch the ingredients?

Keil and Delitzsch state the doctrine the verse carries. The people had no shortcoming in the matter of sacrifice; but in this service, being mere outward service of works, the Lord has no pleasure if the heart is estranged from him and rebels against his commandments, and here is the teaching that to obey is better than sacrifice. Calvin says the same in his own idiom, that the prophet replies to hypocrites who thought they made expiation when they had offered incense and sacrifices, as though that were all that serving God required; they mocked God with their fopperies and reckoned him extremely cruel when he was not satisfied with externals, and the temple became on this account a den of thieves.

The stumbling-blocks are identified by two and read grammatically by a third. Keil and Delitzsch make them the inroads of the enemies whose formidableness the next verse depicts, and note that the idea of totality is realised by naming individual cases. Calvin compares the near judgments to nets or traps, since the Jews hoped to escape, and puts the sense as a warning that wherever they go they will meet the nets by which God will catch them, so that however they conspire together they will be exposed to the same punishment. Wesley reads the divine part in it carefully, that God will suffer such things to be laid in their way as shall occasion their destruction, and takes the neighbour to mean men of all sorts and conditions. Ellicott corrects the rendering, preferring I give unto this people stumbling-blocks, and they shall stumble over them, with the pairs following as the subjects of the second verb. Gill supplies the ground: their immorality and hypocrisy, their contempt of the word, and their confidence in legal rites.
22:
The people from the north are identified with some hesitation. Gill names the Assyrians from Babylon, which lay north of Judea. Wesley names the Chaldeans, stirred up like a great storm, and glosses the sides of the earth as the uttermost parts of their territories. Ellicott allows a second candidate, saying the words point to the Chaldean and perhaps also to a Scythian invasion, and noting that the northern quarters are used elsewhere of the home of a figure representing the Scythian tribes; he renders the verb literally as roused or awakened and the sides as the ends or far-off regions. Clarke reports the same alternative on the authority of a scholar he names, observing that the Scythians had overrun many parts of Asia before this and spread consternation wherever their name was heard. Keil and Delitzsch simply say a distant and cruel people will execute the judgment, since Judah under trial has proved to be worthless metal. Calvin defends the repeated formula that introduces them: the prophet might have said only that a nation shall come from the north, but he premises that he had the message from God and introduces God as the speaker so that the holy name might rouse their minds more powerfully.

Their armament is described and one word is disputed. Gill says each was furnished with both weapons so as to fight near and afar off, bows to shoot at a distance and spears to strike close, and reports that the Targum renders the second as shields; the cruelty is mentioned, he says, to strike terror into hardened hearts. Calvin rejects the shield outright, on the ground that those who so render it do not attend to the design of the passage, since no mention is made here of defence but only of shooting at a distance, and he notes that three versions render the noun a spear or lance improperly. Ellicott identifies the weapons as the special arms of the Chaldeans and the spear as a javelin shot or hurled, and supplies the evidence for the ferocity, that prisoners impaled or flayed alive or burnt in the furnace were common incidents of their wars and sieges; he adds that cavalry appears to have been a novelty to a people accustomed to war-chariots.
24:
The cry of terror is read as impersonation, and they say whose. Gill takes the report not as the prophet's earlier warning but as the rumour of the enemy's actual approach, and allows the words to be the people's or the prophet's, joining himself with them. Ellicott calls it another dramatic impersonation of the cry of the city's dwellers, the imagery of the woman in travail reproduced from an earlier chapter. Wesley says it briefly: the prophet personates the people's affections. Calvin explains the method again: the prophet draws them against their will into the scene, because plain words could not move hearts settled in contempt.

The warning against going out is glossed practically and then traced forward. Gill takes the field barred for pleasure or business alike, whether walking in it for the air or ploughing and reaping, the danger requiring them to keep within the walls. Ellicott renders the field as the open country and says passing beyond the walls of a beleaguered city would be full of danger, finding a parallel in the gospel discourse. He then makes an observation more notable than it appears: the words fear on every side impressed themselves on the prophet's mind and became a watchword, so that he later gave them as a name to a particular man. Wesley reads it as expressing the danger everywhere. Calvin says the verse confirms the last: the Jews regarded all threatenings as nothing, so had to be constrained to fear by having the scene set before their eyes.

The sackcloth and the ashes divide the readings between repentance and despair. Gill allows either a token of repentance, such as a foreign king and his subjects once made, or a sign of mourning for the calamities coming. Ellicott distinguishes the gestures: the ordinary sign of mourning was to sprinkle dust on the head, whereas wallowing in ashes indicated a more utter prostration; he adds a note on the English verb, once used reflexively and now intransitive. Calvin leaves it open, doubting whether the prophet exhorts to repentance or denounces mourning on the irreclaimable, and defends the length of the passage: he seems to extend his discourse too far, but could not rouse the Jews without great vehemence.

The tower is the tile's real crux, and it turns on a rare word. Gill offers two senses: a watch-tower from which to observe the people and descry the enemy, or a trier, since the word comes from one signifying to try metals, which he thinks likelier because the metaphor is carried on afterwards. Ellicott calls the verse difficult, containing words found nowhere else and therefore guessed at, and gives the recent commentators' rendering, as a prover of ore I have set thee among my people, which agrees with the metallurgical imagery that follows; he records the alternative that keeps the fortress. Calvin takes the other side and argues from word order: since the term for fortress follows, the first word can only be a citadel or rampart, and he has no doubt a citadel for watching is meant. Keil and Delitzsch keep tower and fortress together. Clarke goes furthest into the metallurgy. Following a scholar he names, he translates that the prophet is appointed to make an assay among the people, and describes the process: the cupel is a broad iron ring filled with the ashes of burnt bones, and lead is added to separate the alloy, so that when all is fused the cupel absorbs the lead and with it the dross, leaving the silver pure on top. Wesley alone reads the verse as encouragement to the prophet rather than a description of his office: God had made him a fortified tower so he might be safe notwithstanding every attempt, and had given him prudence to see what is amiss and undauntedness to oppose it.
28:
The verdict on the people is stated as a Hebrew superlative and read out by two. Ellicott renders the phrase literally as rebels of rebels, a Hebraism for the worst rebellion, notes that walking with slanders was a common expression pointing to the tale-bearer's restless eagerness to spread falsehoods, and glosses the two metals as base ones serving vile uses, the imagery made familiar by an earlier prophet. Keil and Delitzsch give the same superlative and settle the root the disputed word comes from. Gill says only that the revolt is from the right way of God and his worship. Calvin explains why the verdict comes here rather than at the beginning: had the prophet said it at first, either the people's fury would have been kindled or his judgment treated with contempt, but coming as what God had known through his servant it had more weight, and the fury was repressed.

The burnt bellows is the tile's crux and the readings split three ways. Gill reports a Jewish commentator, followed by the Targum, interpreting them as the prophet's own mouth and throat, dried up and hoarse through reproving the people to no profit. Calvin reports the same and marks it as what interpreters generally do, referring the whole to the teaching and making the prophet's mouth the bellows by which the fire was kindled, so that he complains his throat had dried like a bellows continually used and at last consumed. Wesley takes it the same way: the prophets had spent their breath to no purpose and their strength was consumed, the judgments heavy as lead are wasted, and the artist may use his greatest skill in vain. Ellicott offers a different construction of the figure. The bellows answer to the life of the prophet as filled with the breath of God, so that he is consumed with that blast and yet his work is faulty; on the next clause he prefers from their fire is lead only, or by another punctuation, the bellows burn with fire yet lead is the only outcome, the point being that lead was used as a flux in smelting silver ore. Keil and Delitzsch state the result rather than the figure: the trial has brought no purification and no separation of the wicked, the whole viewed as a long but resultless smelting; they also propose breaking one word into two, following the margin, since no feminine form of the kind otherwise occurs.

The final verdict is agreed, and the disagreement is only about who pronounces it. Gill reports that the Targum and three ancient versions read the verb as an imperative, call ye them, and explains why the name is apt: the Jews thought themselves of some account as silver, being the seed of Abraham and having the law and covenant, but those who tried them found nothing but dross, so that if they must be called silver they could be called no other than reprobate. Ellicott prefers the marginal refuse silver, the dross and not the metal, so worthless that even God as the great refiner rejects it as yielding nothing; the adjective and the verb, he notes, are formed from the same root, refuse silver because God has refused them. Keil and Delitzsch put it as the final statement of the case, that they are recognised as rejected silver because God has given over trying to make anything of them. Wesley glosses the term commercially, such as will be rejected in payments. Calvin closes on the concession the word silver involves: cast a hundred times into the furnace they would not be improved, never softened on account of their hopeless obstinacy, and they were not worthy of the name at all; but the prophets often conceded something to hypocrites, not without the appearance of a taunt, as here, since the Jews wished to be regarded as silver.
